title: Wafer-scale DRAM carpet bonded beneath a wafer-scale accelerator
idea: Jump from die stacks to whole wafers: hybrid-bond an entire 300 mm DRAM wafer face-to-face under a wafer-scale logic wafer at 2 um pitch, so every compute tile owns the ~50 mm2 of DRAM directly beneath it through millions of vertical links. Dead DRAM tiles are fused out by a wafer-level map and the tile above borrows its neighbor's memory over the on-wafer mesh.
why: Deletes HBM TSVs, interposer and PHYs (facts 5, 6): vertical hops at ~0.05 pJ/bit vs 3-4 pJ/bit, and DRAM area per bit returns to DDR5-like with no 3x TSV tax.

title: Capillary droplet self-alignment for sub-micron chiplet-to-wafer hybrid bonding
idea: Shift alignment from a multi-million-dollar robot to molecular-scale surface tension: hydrophilic pad patterns plus a water droplet pull each DRAM chiplet into register to <200 nm as the droplet evaporates, then Cu/oxide direct bonding locks it. A coarse +/-10 um pick-and-place is enough because the liquid does the last mile.
why: Cuts hybrid-bonding tool capital ~5-10x and raises throughput ~10x, making 1-2 um pitch DRAM-on-logic affordable for U.S. OSATs (capital intensity, U.S. manufacturability, pJ/bit).

title: Ultra-wide 200 MHz near-threshold interface with 64k wires per stack
idea: Shift the link's timescale 30x slower and its width 30x wider: with 3 um hybrid bonds a stack exposes 64k data pads clocked at 200 MHz with 0.2 V swing, driven by plain CMOS inverters with no SerDes, DFE, PLL or termination. Bandwidth matches HBM4 while each bit only charges ~20 fF of micron-length wire.
why: Interface energy falls from 3-4 pJ/bit to ~0.03-0.05 pJ/bit (fact 5) and PHY area on base and host dies shrinks ~5x.

title: Wavelength-as-address: laser comb line selects the DRAM bank group
idea: Move the address decoder from nanometer on-die wiring to the rack-scale photonic spectrum: each bank group has a micro-ring receiver tuned to one comb line, so the host addresses memory by choosing which wavelength carries the request and data. One 64-line comb on a single fiber replaces 64 point-to-point links and the bank-select decode tree.
why: Attacks periphery area (fact 7) and rack-scale data movement (fact 5): fewer fibers and SerDes per GB and ~1 pJ/bit optical memory access at meter reach.

title: Ceiling MEMS free-space optics re-wire stranded rack DRAM per job phase
idea: Treat the datacenter ceiling as a memory backplane: MEMS steering mirrors link any compute sled to any memory sled with free-space optical beams, re-pointed in ~10 ms at job-phase boundaries that last seconds to minutes. DRAM stranded behind an idle CPU is lent to the busy GPU one row over.
why: Raises usable memory supply: 20-30% of datacenter DRAM is typically stranded, and recovering it is equivalent to new fab output with zero wafer capex.

title: Liquid-metal micro-sockets let interposers outlive three DRAM generations
idea: Shift packaging lifetime from one product cycle to a decade: HBM stacks seat into polymer wells filled with gallium-indium alloy at ~20 um pitch, held by a clamp, so stacks lift out at room temperature for swap, upgrade or redeployment. The costly logic die and interposer persist while memory rotates.
why: Raises effective supply and cuts embodied capital: good HBM is no longer scrapped with the accelerator, giving ~2-3x more service years per stack.

title: Refresh-by-migration: refresh rows by moving them to their next tier
idea: Fuse the 64 ms refresh timescale with the tiering timescale: instead of activating rows only to rewrite them in place, the controller reads rows due for refresh out over the link and writes them to their new home (hot rows up toward on-package, cold rows down to pooled memory). Mandated refresh activations become free migration bandwidth.
why: Converts ~46 fJ/bit refresh spend (fact 3) into useful placement work and cuts separate migration traffic by ~30-50% in tiered memory systems.

title: Liner-free ruthenium nano-TSVs at 300 nm through 5 um dies
idea: Shrink the TSV ~20x in diameter: ruthenium needs no diffusion barrier and keeps low resistivity at small cross-sections, so dies thinned to 5 um get 300 nm Ru vias at 1 um pitch instead of 5-10 um Cu TSVs with large keep-out zones. Vias drop into the array region instead of a dedicated TSV stripe.
why: Attacks the HBM TSV tax (fact 6): TSV plus keep-out area falls >90%, moving HBM area per bit from ~3x toward ~1.3x DDR5, and lower via capacitance trims pJ/bit.

title: Sense-amp-direct bonding: data exits each bank vertically, skipping global I/O
idea: Jump the data path from millimeter global I/O lines to micrometer vertical hops: each bank's sense-amp stripe carries its own fine-pitch hybrid-bond field to the logic die above, so column data leaves exactly where it is sensed. Column muxes, global data lines and the center-strip I/O block disappear.
why: On-die global data movement is a large slice of the 3-4 pJ/bit (fact 5) and of periphery (fact 7); ~40-60% lower access energy and ~10-15% die area returned to cells.

title: Resonant LC tank bus recycles CV2 energy every clock cycle
idea: Match the bus to a resonant timescale: inductors integrated in the interposer let the wide bus's wire capacitance swing inside an LC tank, with data encoded on an adiabatic sinusoidal clock-power line. Charge sloshes back between L and C each cycle instead of being dumped to ground.
why: Breaks the CV2 floor on interface energy (facts 5, 10): ~50-70% lower energy for wide parallel memory buses.

title: 600 mm glass panel interposers with embedded silicon memory bridges
idea: Jump the interposer from a 300 mm wafer to a 600x600 mm glass panel: through-glass vias and multilevel RDL are made on LCD-fab tools, and small silicon bridges are embedded only under the HBM-to-logic edges. One panel yields ~5x the interposer area of a wafer at LCD-class cost per m2.
why: Cuts 2.5D packaging cost and capital ~3-5x with tools that are not EUV-bound and can be built in the U.S.

title: Second-life HBM: laser-debond retired stacks into CXL memory cards
idea: Stretch the stack's timescale from a 3-year accelerator life to 10 years: retired accelerators have their HBM laser-debonded, re-bumped and mounted on a cheap organic carrier beside a small CXL controller ASIC that speaks the HBM PHY. Each card becomes a 100+ GB pooled memory device.
why: Adds usable supply with no wafers: millions of HBM stacks retire each year, and reuse costs a small fraction of new bits.

title: Function-shipping packets: memory requests carry bytecode run at the hub
idea: Invert the scale of what moves: instead of hauling gigabytes to the CPU, each CXL request carries a ~64-byte verified bytecode (filter, gather, reduce) that a tiny core on the memory hub executes, returning only the result. The fabric moves kernels, not data.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5) drops 10-100x for gather and scan-heavy work, and fewer bits in flight shrink the DRAM needed for staging buffers.

title: Passive silicon interposer becomes a trench-capacitor memory layer
idea: Exploit the scale of an otherwise idle ~2500 mm2 65 nm silicon interposer: etch deep-trench capacitors and simple access transistors into its unused area to form ~0.5-1 GB of eDRAM microns from the logic. It acts as a giant page buffer between HBM and compute.
why: Adds memory on a mature, non-EUV, U.S.-capable node (fact 4) at <1 pJ/bit and filters ~20-40% of HBM traffic.

title: Package cavity as a 300 GHz waveguide for wireless DRAM broadcast
idea: Shift from wires to a millimeter-scale electromagnetic cavity: the sealed metal package lid forms a waveguide, each DRAM die carries an on-chip 300 GHz antenna, requests are broadcast to all dies and replies use frequency slots. Only power needs physical vertical connections.
why: Removes data TSVs (fact 6), simplifying stacking yield and enabling die-to-die multicast at a ~1 pJ/bit target.

title: Address-free scheduled-stream DRAM programmed at compile time
idea: Shift address generation from runtime nanoseconds to compile time: for AI graphs the whole access sequence is known, so the compiler loads a compact access program into the stack's base die, which streams rows in order with no command/address traffic. The host simply consumes a tape.
why: Eliminates command/address bus pins and energy and lets each row be activated once and fully consumed, attacking 128x overfetch (fact 8) and bus energy (fact 5): ~20-30% interface energy saved.

title: Phase-change heat-sponge interlayers enable 24-high stacks for burst seconds
idea: Use the thermal timescale (seconds) as a design variable: thin sealed micro-cells of low-melt Bi-In alloy between DRAM dies melt during training bursts and refreeze during communication lulls. Peaks are buffered rather than conducted, so taller stacks stay within temperature limits.
why: Stack height is thermally capped; 24-high instead of 12-16-high raises GB per package footprint ~1.5-2x without more interposer beachfront (fact 6).

title: DRAM in the socket cavity on the CPU package underside
idea: Use the package's other face: LPDDR packages mount on the land side of the CPU substrate inside a cavity in the socket and motherboard, putting memory ~2 mm under the die instead of 5 cm away on DIMMs. The top side stays free for cooling.
why: The short channel runs unterminated at ~1-2 pJ/bit vs 10-20 pJ/bit for DDR5 (fact 5) while keeping DRAM out of the logic die's heat path.

title: Liquid-nitrogen memory backplane: 77 K copper for passive 2 m links
idea: Shift the temperature scale to change wire physics: memory sleds and backplane sit in LN2, where copper resistivity drops ~7x, so passive 2 m memory channels need no retimers or heavy equalization, and DRAM retention stretches to seconds so refresh nearly vanishes.
why: Rack-scale pooled-memory link energy drops ~3-5x and refresh (fact 3) nearly disappears, traded against cryocooling overhead.

title: Clockless delay-insensitive DRAM interface eliminating DLLs and PLLs
idea: Abandon the global nanosecond clock: data moves with dual-rail or level-encoded handshakes so each transfer completes when it completes, and the DRAM drops its DLL, which burns power even when idle. Bus speed tracks voltage and temperature automatically.
why: Removes DLL/PLL standby power and worst-case timing guard bands: ~20-30% lower interface energy at low utilization.

title: Micro-LED imaging-fiber links move HBM a meter from the accelerator
idea: Scale HBM's parallelism into optics: a 2D array of hundreds of micro-LEDs and photodiodes couples into a coherent imaging fiber bundle, each pixel a 2-4 Gb/s lane, so a stack can sit a meter away at HBM-class width with no lasers or SerDes.
why: Frees accelerator beachfront (fact 6) and enables pooled HBM at ~1 pJ/bit (fact 5) with memory cooled separately from the GPU.

title: U.S. hybrid-bond HBM assembly from imported known-good DRAM wafers
idea: Shift the U.S. entry point from the 5-year fab scale to the 18-month packaging scale: tariff-exempt imports of tested DRAM wafers feed U.S.-built hybrid-bonding and stacking lines backed by investment tax credits, producing HBM and DRAM-on-logic domestically; front-end fabs follow once demand is captive.
why: Raises U.S. manufacturability fast (U.S. makes 1-2% of DRAM): packaging lines cost ~$1-2B vs $15B+ fabs and capture ~30-40% of HBM value.

title: Nanotwinned-copper 150 C bonding stacks DRAM without retention loss
idea: Shift the bonding time-temperature budget down an order of magnitude: (111)-oriented nanotwinned Cu pads diffuse fast enough to bond at ~150 C in minutes, avoiding the 300-400 C anneals that degrade access-transistor leakage. DRAM can then be bonded onto finished logic without a retention penalty.
why: Protects the retention tail (fact 3) during 3D stacking, raising stack yield and trimming refresh guard bands.

title: Row-scale LDPC: decode the whole 8 KB activated row at once
idea: Shift the ECC codeword from 64 bits to the 64 Kb row that activation already drags out: a rate-0.85 LDPC code spans each row and a pipeline in the base die decodes it as the row lands in the buffer. A 1% raw cell BER drops below 1e-15 with ~15% parity (BSC capacity at 1% is 0.92).
why: Turns 128x overfetch (fact 8) into an asset; tolerating 1% BER permits ~4-8x longer refresh (fact 3) and smaller capacitors (fact 1).

title: GPU tensor cores decode memory codewords so the base die stays dumb
idea: Move error correction across scales, from a small base-die ASIC to the accelerator's idle matrix engines: stacks ship raw 1%-BER codewords with parity, and the GPU runs batched min-sum LDPC decoding on tensor cores in the shadow of other loads. The stack's base die can then be built on the DRAM process with no logic node.
why: Lets cells run at 1% BER while removing the costly logic-process base die (fact 6, capital); decoding costs ~1-3% of GPU throughput.

title: Two-threshold sensing exports erasure flags over a side channel
idea: Shift from binary to graded certainty at the cell-to-wire boundary: sense amps resolve twice with offset references, marking gray-zone cells as erasures, and a sparse erasure bitmap travels beside the data. Erasure decoding corrects ~2x more than blind errors, so a 1% raw BER needs only ~8% parity.
why: Halves ECC overhead for 1%-BER cells, preserving density while enabling lower VARY (fact 10).

title: Deferred linear correction: compute on raw weights, subtract error product later
idea: Exploit matmul linearity to shift correction in time: the accelerator multiplies immediately with raw 1%-BER weights (exponent bits ride in a protected lane), while the decoder later emits a sparse error matrix E, and the output is fixed by subtracting E*x at ~1-2% of the original work.
why: Removes ~10-20 ns of decode latency from every HBM read and lets cheap 1%-BER cells feed accelerators at full speed.

title: Bit-significance stack: MSB planes on clean dies, LSB planes on cheap dies
idea: Shift the unit of placement from the word to the bit-plane along the stack's vertical axis: sign, exponent and high-mantissa planes go to 4 protected dies, low-order planes go to 8 dies running at 1% BER with no ECC, and the base die re-interleaves planes into words on the fly.
why: Two-thirds of bits live on refresh-relaxed, low-voltage dies (facts 3, 10) with <0.1% model-quality loss; precision-on-demand fetching also cuts data moved up to ~50%.

title: Bond-pad interleaving makes 1% dead hybrid bonds correctable
idea: Shift the error budget from the cell scale to the bond scale: each codeword's bits are spread across many hybrid-bond pads, so a pad lost to a particle or void looks like scattered bit errors that the 1%-tolerant code already fixes. Bonding then runs with relaxed cleanliness and planarity and no spare-pad repair.
why: HBM yield is down 20-30% (fact 6); defect-tolerant bonding recovers most of it and permits cheaper bonders and less cleanroom.

title: B-grade die recapture: weak-cell DRAM fallout into heavy-ECC stacks
idea: Move the pass/fail line from zero unrepairable bits to <=1% weak cells: dies that fab test would scrap or down-bin are stacked on a heavy-LDPC base die and sold as full-capacity memory, with a buyer contracting for fab fallout at scrap-plus prices.
why: Raises usable bit supply from existing wafers ~5-15% (typical DRAM yield loss) with zero new fab capex.

title: Graceful capacity decay: code rate grows as modules age
idea: Stretch the memory's timescale to a decade: the base die tracks raw BER as cells wear and leak (up to 1% and beyond), automatically raising parity and announcing a slightly lower capacity through a hot-capacity-change event the OS honors. Modules retire only when ~15% capacity is gone.
why: Roughly doubles service life of deployed DRAM/HBM, effectively adding supply, and lets new parts ship with thinner margins.

title: Noise-trained models let inference memory strip all ECC
idea: Shift the error budget from access time (ns) to training time (hours): models are trained with injected 1% bit flips on stored weights and KV entries, with exponent clamping, so inference memory runs with zero parity, zero decode latency and unprotected cheap cells.
why: Recovers the ~12.5% capacity and bandwidth spent on ECC bits and lets inference memory use 1%-BER cells with relaxed refresh (fact 3).

title: TTL-tagged writes: rows holding short-lived data skip refresh
idea: Match data lifetime to retention time: every write over the interface carries a time-to-live hint (activations microseconds, KV cache seconds), and rows whose data dies before 1% of cells decay are never refreshed. At 1% tolerance that unrefreshed window stretches from 64 ms to roughly 1 s.
why: Cuts refresh energy and bandwidth loss (fact 3: 16-33% of idle power, 10-20% of bandwidth) ~70-90% for AI working sets.

title: Rack-shared scrub appliance replaces per-device heavy decoders
idea: Shift heavy correction to rack scale and hour timescale: long-retention memory devices carry only a light access-path decoder sized for 1% raw BER, while one rack-level appliance with powerful soft decoders sweeps every pool over CXL in low-load hours, rewriting rows before drift pushes errors past 1%. Refresh becomes an hourly network service.
why: Amortizes decoder silicon across hundreds of devices and replaces ms-scale refresh (fact 3) with hourly scrubbing for long-retention cells.

title: Cell-to-wire PAM: 2-bit analog cells drive the link undigitized
idea: Collapse two signaling scales into one: each cell holds four charge levels, and the sense path forwards its level directly as a PAM-4 symbol over the short hybrid-bonded link, where the host slicer makes the only decision. Cell and link noise merge into one 1% symbol-error budget decoded once.
why: ~2x bits per cell, sidestepping the charge wall (fact 1) by tolerating level errors, and half the wire transitions per bit (~40% less interface energy).

title: Harvest timing guard bands: cut tRCD and tRP 40% at 1% BER
idea: Shift the access timescale below the worst case: timings set so the slowest cell at the hottest corner never fails are cut ~40%, letting a few slow cells mis-sense and the row code absorb them.
why: ~30-40% lower random-access latency and higher bank throughput, so fewer stacks deliver a target bandwidth.

title: Charge-pump-free single-rail stack frees power TSVs and periphery
idea: Collapse the die's multi-rail scheme into one package-level ~0.7 V rail: the ~3 V wordline boost and 1 V array rail go away, and the resulting ~1% sensing and leakage errors from weaker access transistors are absorbed by the code. Without VPP pumps and extra regulators the stack needs far fewer power TSVs.
why: Attacks the voltage floor (fact 10, ~2x CV2), periphery (fact 7, pumps and regulators) and TSV area (fact 6, power TSVs are often the majority).

title: Ship untested wafers: skip hours-long retention test and burn-in
idea: Shift testing from the fab's hours-long retention screens and burn-in ovens to the field's nanosecond decoder: wafers go from light probe straight to bonding, and the base die learns per-row error statistics online.
why: Test and burn-in cost ~5-10% of cost per bit and weeks of cycle time; dropping them frees test-floor capital and speeds supply.

title: lossy_malloc: cloud memory tier priced by tolerated bit error rate
idea: Create a datacenter-scale market: the allocator exposes lossy_malloc(ber=1e-2), mapping those pages onto pools with 1%-BER cells, B-grade dies or relaxed refresh at ~1/3 the price, and frameworks place embeddings, KV caches and media buffers there by default.
why: Creates demand for cheap error-tolerant capacity, multiplying usable supply for AI and media without new fabs.

title: Predictive link sends only surprises, leaving sub-1% residual errors
idea: Shift from sending bits to sending surprises: identical predictors (previous value plus learned delta) run at both ends of the memory link and only mispredicted bits are sent; since consumers already absorb 1% cell errors, the predictor may be lossy and residual mismatches are simply not retransmitted.
why: ~2-4x effective link bandwidth for smooth tensor streams (fact 5), cutting pJ per useful bit proportionally.

title: Hot-stack: DRAM bonded straight onto a 1 kW GPU at 125 C
idea: Shift the thermal scale: retention collapses at high temperature, which is why DRAM is kept off hot logic, but with 1% tolerance and row-scale codes DRAM dies can be hybrid-bonded directly on the GPU die at 115-125 C with refresh only modestly raised.
why: Deletes the interposer and HBM PHY (facts 5, 6): memory-on-logic at ~0.1 pJ/bit in the tightest possible package.

title: Contactless capacitive stacking through 1 um dies, link errors folded in
idea: Replace data TSVs with capacitive couplers across dies thinned to ~1 um: the coupled signal is marginal (raw link BER ~1e-3), but it is simply added to the 1% cell error budget and corrected by the same code. Dies join by oxide-oxide fusion bonding, with only a few large vias for power.
why: Removes most TSV area and yield tax (fact 6: 3x area, -20-30% yield); oxide-only bonding is cheaper and more defect-tolerant than Cu-Cu hybrid bonding.

title: Glass-panel substrate memory: multi-tier oxide TFT cells in package RDL
idea: Jump to display-panel scale: the 600 mm glass package substrate is built on LCD lines with 8 tiers of IGZO thin-film-transistor capacitor cells in its redistribution layers, giving a few GB per package of working memory; the ~1% BER from TFT variation is absorbed by row codes in the logic die.
why: Adds non-EUV, U.S.-buildable capacity on LCD-class capital (fact 4) right next to the logic die.

title: Hadamard-spread embedding storage turns bit flips into faint Gaussian noise
idea: Shift the unit of meaning from bits to whole vectors: embeddings are stored after a fixed Hadamard rotation and spread-spectrum quantization, so any 1% of flipped bits perturb every coordinate slightly instead of wrecking a few; the inverse transform runs in the near-memory logic die as data streams out.
why: Lets the largest AI capacity consumers (recommendation tables, retrieval indexes, KV caches) live in no-ECC 1%-BER memory with negligible accuracy loss, ~2x lower cost per usable bit.

title: Z-channel coding exploits one-way charge leakage at the interface encoder
idea: Use the physics timescale of leakage: retention errors almost only turn stored charge to no-charge, so the interface encoder maps data to true/anti-cell polarity to minimize charged cells and applies an asymmetric (Z-channel) code. At 1% one-directional error, capacity rises from 0.92 to ~0.95 and parity needs fall ~40%.
why: Cuts ECC overhead for 1%-BER cells and reduces charged-cell count (refresh and CV2 energy, facts 3, 10) by ~20-30%.

title: Vertical product codes striped through the stack's TSV columns
idea: Rotate part of the codeword 90 degrees: each die keeps a horizontal row code for its 1% cell errors, and a vertical Reed-Solomon code places one symbol per die along the same TSV column, so a dead TSV or an entire failed die becomes a correctable erasure in the same structure.
why: Raises HBM stack yield (fact 6, -20-30%) toward ~95% while tolerating 1% cell BER and removing redundancy rows and repair fuses from periphery (fact 7).
